title: Blind tasting
subtitle: Reasoning from the glass
objectives: Explain how to approach a blind tasting
Use evidence from appearance, nose and palate

steps.title: Evidence first
steps.body: Blind tasting is reasoning, not guessing. Gather evidence: colour, aroma intensity and families, structure. Then ask what it suggests. Deep colour suggests thick skins or warmth. High acidity suggests a cool climate or a high-acid grape. Oak suggests ambition and price. Each clue narrows the options.

steps.title: Narrowing down
steps.body: Build the argument in steps. Is it Old World or New World? Fruit-forward and ripe suggests New World or warm sites; earthy, savoury and restrained suggests Old World or cool sites. Then climate: cool, moderate or warm. Then grape. Then region and age. Stop when the evidence runs out, rather than forcing an answer.

steps.prompt: A red is pale ruby, high acidity, low tannin, red cherry and earthy notes. What is the most likely conclusion?
steps.explanation: Pale colour, low tannin, high acidity and earthiness point to a cool-climate Pinot Noir, like Burgundy.

steps.body: In blind tasting, the first impression is often right, but say why. If you can't justify a guess with evidence from the glass, keep looking.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of a blind conclusion in order.
items: Decide Old World or New World
steps.explanation: Each step narrows the possibilities using the evidence before it.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Blind tasting is reasoning from evidence
Narrow from world to climate, grape, region and age
Stop when the evidence runs out
